rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blessing of the Lord may refer to the Prophet’s prophethood.
rows.anchor: The blessing of thy Lord may be a reference to prophethood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial that the Prophet is possessed directly answers the disbelievers’ charge in 15:6–7.
rows.anchor: verse’s assertion that the Prophet is not possessed can be seen as a direct response to the derogatory statement of the disbelievers in 15:6–7

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some interpret “exalted character” as describing the religion of Islam.
rows.anchor: Some interpret exalted character as a descriptor of the religion of Islam (IK, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most understand the verse as describing the Prophet, whose character was exalted because his only aspiration was God.
rows.anchor: but most associate it with the Prophet himself; his character is said to be exalted because he had no aspiration other than God (Q)

rows.speaker: ʿĀʾishah
rows.claim: Asked about the Prophet’s character, ʿĀʾishah said that his character was the Quran.
rows.anchor: The Prophet’s wife ʿĀʾishah was once asked about the Prophet’s character and responded, “Do you not read the Quran? . . . His character was the Quran”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khuluq, “character,” is closely related to khalq, the Quran’s primary word for “creation.”
rows.anchor: Character translates khuluq, which is closely related to the primary Quranic word for “creation”

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet prayed that God beautify his character as God had beautified his created form.
rows.anchor: it is reported that the Prophet used to pray, “O God you have beautified my created form

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet said that his mission was to perfect noble character traits.
rows.anchor: Another ḥadīth states, “I was only sent to perfect the noble traits of character”

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet taught that the best people are those with the best character traits.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is also reported to have enjoined good character traits upon his followers, saying, “The best of you are those who are best in character

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet enjoined reverence of God, following bad deeds with good ones, and treating people with good character.
rows.anchor: The Prophet is also reported to have enjoined good character traits upon his followers

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet said that beauty of character is what most admits people into Paradise.
rows.anchor: “What admits people most into Paradise is beauty of character”

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet said good character weighs heavily on a believer’s scales and can raise one to the rank of those who pray and fast.
rows.anchor: “Nothing is placed on the scales of a believer that is weightier than beauty of character; and one who has beauty of character will reach thereby the degree of one who prays and fasts”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beautiful character can be understood as the opposite of the state of being possessed mentioned in verse 2.
rows.anchor: those with beautiful character traits are far from the state of being possessed referred to in verse 2 (Āl)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The deniers are the Makkan disbelievers who urged the Prophet and his followers to follow their forefathers’ religion instead of the revelation.
rows.anchor: The deniers refers to the Makkan disbelievers who were bidding the Prophet and his followers to follow the religion of their forefathers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dāhana can mean “to demean,” “to deny,” or “to take something lightly.”
rows.anchor: Compromise translates the verb dahana, which can mean both “to demean” and “to deny” or “to take something lightly.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading has the disbelievers ready to compromise if the Prophet and his followers compromise; another has them already compromising and wanting believers to do likewise.
rows.anchor: will compromise when the Prophet and his followers compromise or that the disbelievers are already compromising; so they want the believers to compromise too (Z)

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: On the first reading, disbelievers would trade concessions in religion or take turns worshipping one another’s gods.
rows.anchor: that the believers worship their gods for a while and then they worship the believers’ God for a while (Bg)

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: On the second reading, the disbelievers want believers to become disbelievers too.
rows.anchor: it means that they are disbelievers; so they wish for believers to become disbelievers as well (Bg)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shank being laid bare is an idiom for a very serious and severe situation.
rows.anchor: The shank is laid bare is an idiomatic expression indicating something very serious and severe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In strenuous effort or battle, Arabs rolled up their garments to expose the shank; the idiom “war broke out upon the shank” means war began vehemently.
rows.anchor: he begins by rolling up his garment in such a fashion that his shank is exposed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arabic idiom “war broke out upon the shank” means that war broke out with vehemence.
rows.anchor: “The war broke out upon the shank,” meaning “The war broke out with vehemence”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some exegetes say God exposes His own Shank to signal the beginning of the Judgment process.
rows.anchor: Some exegetes say that in this verse it is God Who exposes His own Shank to signal the beginning of the judgment process

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: A variant reading, “We lay bare the shank,” makes God the one who exposes it.
rows.anchor: meaning God (Q). Others say the shank is laid bare

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others understand the shank being laid bare as the unveiling of secrets.
rows.anchor: Others say the shank is laid bare refers to the secrets that will be unveiled.

rows.speaker: ḥadīth
rows.claim: A report says God will expose His Shank; sincere believers will prostrate, while those who performed prayer for show will be unable, their backs stiffened like a plate.
rows.anchor: a ḥadīth states, “God will lay bare His Shank and then the believers, men and women, will prostrate before Him

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: A third reading, “It lays bared the shank,” means the Resurrection exposes great severities.
rows.anchor: meaning that the Resurrection exposes great severities (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although some Arabs considered the bodily position of prostration humiliating, the disbelievers will face greater humiliation in the Hereafter and be unable to prostrate.
rows.anchor: but in the Hereafter the disbelievers will find much greater humiliation and be unable to prostrate, as mentioned in v. 42

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the prostration in both verses as prostration for prayer in worldly life.
rows.anchor: references to prostrating for prayer in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes verse 42 as prostration on Judgment Day and verse 43 as the worldly call to prayer that the disbelievers ignored; their later inability follows from refusing to prostrate when sound.
rows.anchor: v. 42 as a reference to prostration on the Day of Judgment and v. 43 as a reference to those who did not heed the call to prostration, meaning to prayer, in this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭāghiyah denotes utmost severity and may indicate Thamūd’s calamity: a cry, earthquake, or thunderbolt.
rows.anchor: Overwhelming translates ṭāghiyah, which implies something that reaches the utmost severity

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Ṭāghiyah can also mean rebellion or upheaval, from ṭughyān.
rows.anchor: It could also mean “rebellion” or “upheaval” (ṭughyān; R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A calamity describes how Thamūd were destroyed, while rebellion describes their sinfulness; the two explanations can both apply.
rows.anchor: the reference to “rebellion” indicates that they were destroyed by their own sinfulness, though the two are not mutually exclusive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭāghiyah may mean those who overwhelmed or oppressed Thamūd: a powerful minority or individual persuaded them to hamstring God’s she-camel and leave her for dead.
rows.anchor: “overwhelmed,” by a powerful minority or a single individual who enjoined them to hamstring the she-camel of God (91:13)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Ṣarṣar describes either a noisy wind or a wind so cold that it feels as if it burns.
rows.anchor: Howling translates ṣarṣar, which indicates either a wind that makes a severe noise or a wind so cold that it feels as if it burns (R)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Some say the wind pierced through to the people’s hearts.
rows.anchor: In this context, some say that it pierced through to their hearts (IK)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: ʿĀtiyah means the wind overwhelmed the people so they could find no cover and was utmost in strength and severity.
rows.anchor: Raging translates ʿātiyah, which indicates both that it overcame the people in such a manner that they could find no cover and that it was the utmost in strength and severity (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ʿĀd wind is also described as howling in 41:16 and 54:19 and as barren in 51:41.
rows.anchor: The tribe of ʿĀd is also reported to have been destroyed by a howling wind in 41:16 and 54:19 and by the barren wind in 51:41

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage shifts from the destruction of pre-Islamic Arabian disbelievers to opponents of prophets in the Judeo-Christian tradition.
rows.anchor: These verses mark a shift from the discussion of the afflictions that befell the disbelievers from pre-Islamic Arabian tribes to those who disbelieved in prophets of the Judeo-Christian tradition

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those before him” can mean the generations preceding Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: Those before him indicates the generations before Pharaoh

rows.speaker: IK, R
rows.claim: With different voweling, wa man qibalahu can mean those who were with Pharaoh, namely his followers.
rows.anchor: “those who were with him,” meaning those who followed Pharaoh (IK, R)

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: “Those subverted” most likely refers to the inhabitants of Sodom and Gomorrah, to whom Lot was sent.
rows.anchor: to the inhabitants of Sodom and Gomorrah, to whom Lot had been sent as a messenger (R, Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The messenger of their Lord may be Moses, Lot, or both.
rows.anchor: The messenger of their Lord could refer to Moses, Lot, or both (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rusūl may mean “message” (risālah), allowing the verse to refer to any disbelieving peoples mentioned in the sūrah.
rows.anchor: which case the verse may refer to any of the disbelieving peoples mentioned in this sūrah

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Rābiyah indicates increase and can mean a punishment surpassing all others.
rows.anchor: Devastating translates rābiyah, which indicates increase, suggesting either a punishment that surpasses that of all others (Q, R)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: It can mean punishment devastating in this world but even more severe in the Hereafter, as with Noah’s people, drowned and then made to enter the Fire.
rows.anchor: more severe in the Hereafter, as with those who disbelieved in Noah: They were drowned, then made to enter a Fire (71:25; R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The overflowing waters allude to Noah’s Flood and Ark.
rows.anchor: These verses are taken as an allusion to Noah’s Ark

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We carried you” means God carried the people’s forefathers while they were still in their descendants’ loins.
rows.anchor: We carried you means We carried your forefathers while you were still in their loins

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reminder may refer to the ship mentioned in verse 11.
rows.anchor: The it in make it a reminder in v. 12 can be taken as a reference to the ship in v. 11

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the reminder may refer to the Resurrection and Judgment described in this sūrah.
rows.anchor: or to the events of the Day of Resurrection and Judgment that this sūrah describes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reminder is compared with the reminder in 50:37 for those who have a heart or listen attentively.
rows.anchor: V. 12 is similar to 50:37: Truly in that is a reminder for whosoever has a heart, or gives ear as witness

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: In one account, God commanded the Prophet to draw ʿAlī close, teach him so that he understood, and guaranteed that understanding; then the verse was revealed.
rows.anchor: According to one account, the Prophet said to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, “God has commanded me to draw you closer

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: In the more widespread account, the Prophet asked God to make ʿAlī’s ear one that heeds the reminder.
rows.anchor: the Prophet said, “I asked my

rows.speaker: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
rows.claim: ʿAlī said he never heard anything from the Messenger of God without remembering it.
rows.anchor: and ʿAlī is reported to have said, “I never heard anything from the Messenger of God but that I remembered it”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the symbolic distinction between right and left, the commentary points to 56:8–9.
rows.anchor: For the symbolic distinction between right and left, see 56:8–9c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The book given at Judgment is the record of deeds, discussed in 17:71, 18:49, and 84:7.
rows.anchor: the meaning of the book presented on the Day of Judgment in which one’s deeds are recorded, see 17:71; 18:49; 84:7

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The righteous are also called the companions of the right in 56:27 and 56:38.
rows.anchor: where the righteous are referred to as the companions of the right

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those given their book in the right hand lived conscious of Judgment and prepared for it.
rows.anchor: Those who receive their book in the right hand have spent their life in this world conscious that the Day of Judgment would come and have prepared for it accordingly

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet called those most mindful of death and best prepared for what follows it the most intelligent believers.
rows.anchor: the Prophet replied, “The most frequent in recalling death, and the best prepared for what follows it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Here” is second-person plural, so the speaker addresses a group.
rows.anchor: Here is in the second person plural, indicating that his words are addressed to a group

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other readings have the second-person singular instead of the plural.
rows.anchor: In other readings, it is the second person singular (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ẓanantu is translated “I knew for certain,” though in some contexts the word indicates doubt.
rows.anchor: I knew for certain translates ẓanantu, a word that in some contexts indicates doubt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ẓanantu implies doubt here, the person was not fully certain of the final outcome but followed God’s and the Prophet’s commands and was rewarded.
rows.anchor: If read in this manner, the verse would indicate that one was not entirely certain of the final outcome, but nonetheless followed the commands of God and the Prophet and was rewarded accordingly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise of a contenting life is repeated in 101:7; the commentary also points to 89:28.
rows.anchor: This verse is repeated in 101:7; regarding contentment, see 89:28c

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The clusters hang low so they are easily reached and no one is turned away from them.
rows.anchor: That the clusters are low-hanging indicates that they are readily accessible and no one will be turned away from them (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: ḥadīth
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet saw a cluster of grapes in the Garden and that, had he taken it, people would have eaten from it as long as the world lasted.
rows.anchor: “Verily I saw the Garden and came upon a cluster of grapes. Had I taken it, you would have eaten of it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Garden’s nearby fruits are also described in 55:54 and 76:14.
rows.anchor: Also see 55:54, which speaks of fruits near at hand, and 76:14, which says of the Garden

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The good deeds done during worldly life are the reason for the Garden’s invitation to eat and drink.
rows.anchor: That which you did in the past indicates the good deeds one did while in the life of this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ayām al-khāliyah can mean “empty days,” interpreted as days of fasting.
rows.anchor: which can also mean “empty days,” in which case it is interpreted as a reference to days of fasting (R, Sy)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those given the book in the left hand are cast into Hell for their deeds.
rows.anchor: Those given the book in the left hand will be cast into Hell for their deeds

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of receiving the record from behind the back in 84:10–12 is reconciled by saying the left hand is tied behind the back.
rows.anchor: To reconcile v. 25 and 84:10, commentators say that the left hand will be tied behind the back

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wish not to receive the book may express a desire to avoid punishment altogether.
rows.anchor: Would that I had not been given may imply a desire to avoid punishment altogether

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the shame of seeing one’s deeds may be worse than the Fire’s pain, making it preferable to enter Hell without judgment.
rows.anchor: it may indicate that the shame at witnessing one’s deeds is worse than the pain of the Fire

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: The speaker wishes death had been the final end and that there had been no Resurrection.
rows.anchor: This verse is understood to mean, “Would that death had been the final end, and there had been no Resurrection” (Q, R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The negative mā may instead be interrogative, making the line a rhetorical question: “What has my wealth availed me?”
rows.anchor: The negative particle mā in this verse could also be understood as an interrogative particle, in which case the verse is understood as a rhetorical question

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The line echoes the Quranic theme that worldly advantages usually do not help in the next life; 18:46 contrasts worldly wealth and children with enduring righteous deeds.
rows.anchor: the broader Quranic theme that the things that provide advantages in this world are usually of no avail in the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sulṭāniyah means authority or warrant; its passing means the person no longer controls his destiny and regrets neglecting preparation for the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: My power translates sulṭāniyah, which indicates authority and warrant; that it has passed means that those who receive the book in their left hand no longer have any control over their own destiny

rows.speaker: Q, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: Sulṭān can also mean argument or proof (ḥujjah).
rows.anchor: Here and in other verses, sulṭān also connotes “argument” or “proof” (ḥujjah; Q, R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The person can no longer argue against the Resurrection or defend himself because his limbs testify to his life and he must admit his sin.
rows.anchor: they no longer have any capacity to argue against the reality of the Resurrection or even to argue for themselves

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: The commands to seize and cast the person into Hell are addressed to the angels who govern Hell.
rows.anchor: These verses are a command to the angels who govern Hell (Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the shackles placed on disbelievers and made to course through their bodies in the Hereafter, the commentary points to 36:8.
rows.anchor: Regarding the shackles that will be placed upon the disbelievers and made to course through their bodies in the Hereafter, see 36:8c

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Judgment and Resurrection overwhelm people so completely that each is concerned only for himself, even disregarding his closest companions.
rows.anchor: The Day of Judgment and the Resurrection will be so overwhelming that people will have no concern for anyone except themselves, even for their most loyal companions in earthly life

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Though no one asks about another, all human beings will see one another.
rows.anchor: They will be made to see them is taken to mean that, although they will ask about no one else, all human beings will see one another (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Alternatively, God may show the believers the condition of the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: It may also mean that God shows the believers the state of the disbelievers (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that God shows the angels the condition of all human beings.
rows.anchor: or that God shows the angels the states of all human beings (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The guilty, or those who work evil in 39:47, seek to ransom themselves; other verses say neither earthfuls of gold nor all earthly possessions would be accepted.
rows.anchor: That the guilty, or elsewhere those who work evil (39:47), will seekto ransom themselves on the Day of Judgment

rows.speaker: IK, Ṭ; IK, Q
rows.claim: Faṣīlah, “kin,” may mean one’s tribe or, more specifically, one’s mother.
rows.anchor: one’s tribe (IK, Ṭ) or more specifically one’s mother (IK, Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Nay” denies the possibility of ransom mentioned in the preceding verses.
rows.anchor: Nay denies the possibility of ransom mentioned in the previous verses

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Alternatively, the opening may be translated “Truly it is a churning fire.”
rows.anchor: Alternately, the verse could be translated, “Truly it is a churning fire” (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laẓā is a name for Hell because its flames churn.
rows.anchor: Churning fire translates laẓā, which is considered one of the names of Hell

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The Fire summons those destined for it because in worldly life they turned from obedience, belief in God’s books and messengers, or the truth.
rows.anchor: The Fire will summon those who are destined for it, because during the life of this world they turned away from obedience to God and fled from belief in God’s books and God’s messengers or from the truth (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The Fire then picks out those who turned their backs on the truth in worldly life.
rows.anchor: Then the Fire will pick out those who turned their backs and fled from the truth in the life of this world (IK)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The jinn listened to the Prophet reciting the Quran.
rows.anchor: The jinn listened to the Prophet’s recitation of the Quran (JJ)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: After returning, the jinn are said to have addressed their own community, marveling at and affirming the Quran.
rows.anchor: to their own community of jinn upon their return (JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This event is also identified with the jinn encounter in 46:29–32.
rows.anchor: This event is also said to be the one referred to in 46:29–32

rows.speaker: Bg
rows.claim: “A wondrous Quran” can mean “an amazing Quran,” whose unparalleled eloquence amazed the jinn as it did human beings.
rows.anchor: which is understood as a reference to an unparalleled eloquence that amazed the jinn (Bg)
